docs.summary: The 5 warning signs of a scam call, text, or email, and what to do next.

docs.heading: The 5 warning signs
docs.text:
1. They say you must act right now. Scammers rush you so you don't stop to think. Honest businesses give you time.
2. They say there's a problem, or a prize. "Your account is locked." "There's a charge you didn't make." "You won a prize, just pay a fee." These are common tricks.
3. They ask you to pay in an odd way. Only scammers insist you pay with gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency, or a payment app.
4. They ask for private information. Real government agencies won't call you out of the blue to ask for your Social Security number. Your bank won't text you a link to "confirm" your password.
5. They pretend to be someone you trust. That could be the IRS, Social Security, your bank, a well-known company, or even a grandchild. The name or number on your screen can be faked.

docs.heading: What to do
docs.text:
1. Pause. You never have to decide right away. It's fine to say "I'll call you back."
   - What you'll tap: On a call, tap the red End button. You won't hurt anyone's feelings.
2. Don't tap links or open attachments in a message you weren't expecting.
   - What you'll tap: Nothing in the message. Just close it.
3. Check for yourself. Call the company or person at a number you already know is real, such as the number on the back of your bank card or in your own contacts. Don't use the number or link in the message.
4. Report it. Your report helps stop scammers.
   - Text message: forward it to 7726 (the number spells "SPAM").
   - Email: forward it to reportphishing@apwg.org.
   - Any scam: tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
   - What you'll tap: For a text, press and hold the message, tap More or Forward, then type 7726 as the number to send to.
5. Delete the message after you report it.

docs.title: How to Reset a Forgotten Password Safely
docs.summary: Reset a forgotten password the safe way, without getting locked out or tricked.
docs.heading: The safe steps (any account)
docs.text:
1. Go to the account yourself. Open the app you normally use, or type the website address yourself.
   - What you'll tap: The app's own icon on your home screen. Don't use a link from a text or email you weren't expecting.
2. Tap Sign in, then tap Forgot password?
   - What you'll tap: Small words, usually under the password box.
3. Follow the steps on screen. You'll usually get a code by text or email.
4. Type the code into the app or website.
   - Never tell this code to anyone, even someone who says they're from the company. Real companies won't call you to ask for it.
5. Make a new password. A good one is long. Four or more random words in a row works well, like maple river teacup lantern.
6. Write it down and keep it somewhere safe at home, or save it in a password manager.

docs.summary: Reset a forgotten password the safe way, without getting locked out or tricked.
docs.heading: For an Apple Account (iPhone, iPad, Mac)
docs.text:
1. If you're still signed in on your iPhone or iPad, you can change the password there: open Settings, tap your name, tap Sign-In & Security, then Change Password. You'll use your phone's passcode.
2. If you're not signed in anywhere, look for Forgot password? on the sign-in screen, or go to iforgot.apple.com.
3. You may be asked for your trusted phone number to get a code. If you set up a recovery contact (a family member or friend), they can give you a code too.
If none of that works, Apple has an account recovery process. It can take several days, on purpose, to keep your account safe. Let it finish.

docs.summary: Use the free password manager already built into your phone.
docs.heading: On an iPhone (Passwords app)
docs.text:
1. Open the Passwords app. (On iPhones with older software, open Settings and tap Passwords.)
   - What you'll tap: A gray icon with a white key.
2. Unlock it with your face, fingerprint, or passcode.
3. Tap All to see your saved passwords. Tap a website or app to see its password.
4. To save a new password: When you sign in to a website or app, your iPhone asks "Save Password?" Tap Save.
5. When making a new account: Your iPhone may offer a Strong Password. Tap Use Strong Password. It's saved for you.

docs.summary: Add a second lock to your email and accounts with two-step login.
docs.heading: For your Google Account (Gmail, Android)
docs.text:
1. Open your Google Account: on Android, open Settings, tap Google, then Manage your Google Account. On a computer, go to myaccount.google.com.
2. Tap Security (or Security & sign-in).
3. Under How you sign in to Google, tap Turn on 2-Step Verification (or tap 2-Step Verification, then Turn on).
4. Follow the steps on screen. Google will suggest Google prompts: a message on your phone that you tap Yes to approve.
5. Save backup codes. Google offers a list of one-time codes. Print them or write them down, and keep them somewhere safe at home.

docs.title: How to Make Text Bigger on Your Phone
docs.summary: Make words bigger and easier to read on iPhone or Android.
docs.heading: On an iPhone
docs.text:
1. Find and tap the Settings app.
   - What you'll tap: A gray icon that looks like a set of gears.
2. Tap Display & Brightness.
   - What you'll tap: A line with a small blue icon showing "AA". You may need to scroll down.
3. Tap Text Size.
4. Drag the slider to the right to make text bigger.
   - What you'll tap: Put your finger on the round dot at the bottom of the screen and slide it right. The sample text gets bigger as you go.
5. Want it even bigger? Go back to Settings, tap Accessibility, then Display & Text Size, then Larger Text.
6. Turn on Larger Accessibility Sizes, then drag the slider to the size you like.
   - What you'll tap: A switch next to the words. It turns green when it's on.

docs.heading: Before you start
docs.text:

docs.heading: What is streaming?
docs.text:
Streaming means watching shows and movies over the internet, instead of through a cable wire, a satellite dish, or an antenna.
Each streaming service is like its own TV channel or video store. You open its app on your TV, phone, tablet, or computer, pick something, and it plays right away. Nothing is downloaded or stored. You watch whenever you want, not just when a show is on.
You need two things:
1. Home internet (or a phone data plan, for small screens).
2. A screen with apps: a smart TV, a streaming device like Roku or Fire TV, a phone, a tablet, or a computer.
Most paid services charge each month. You can usually cancel anytime.

docs.heading: Option 1: An antenna for local news (free)
docs.text:
An antenna gets your local stations, like ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC, and PBS, with their local news, weather, and national news shows.
1. See what you can get. Type fcc.gov/media/engineering/dtvmaps into your web browser. Enter your address. You'll see a list of stations near you.
2. Get an antenna. Indoor antennas are sold at most stores that sell TVs. The FCC says your antenna should get both VHF and UHF channels. If the map says your signals are weak, an outdoor antenna works better.
3. Plug it in. Connect the antenna cable to the port on the back of your TV marked ANT IN or Antenna.
4. Scan for channels. Press Menu or Settings on your remote. Look for Channels, then Channel scan or Auto program. Your TV will find the stations.
5. Move it if needed. Moving the antenna a few inches, higher, or near a window can help. Scan again after you move it.
Tip: Scan again every few months. Stations sometimes change, and the FCC suggests rescanning to keep your list up to date.

docs.heading: The honest answer first
docs.text:
- A smart speaker can call family and friends by voice. This can help if you can't reach your phone.
- Most smart speakers can't call 911 on their own. Amazon says that by default, Alexa doesn't support calling 911.
- It needs power and Wi-Fi. If the power or internet is out, it won't work.
- It has to hear you. Running water, a closed door, or a soft voice can get in the way. Test it from the spots where you'd need it.
- A smart speaker is not a medical alert system. A phone or watch with Emergency SOS, or a medical alert service, is made for emergencies.

docs.heading: What is AI?
docs.text:
AI stands for artificial intelligence. It means computer programs that can do tasks that used to need a person, like understanding speech, writing, or recognizing faces in photos.
AI learns by looking at huge amounts of examples, like books, websites, and pictures. Then it uses patterns from those examples to make a guess about what comes next. It doesn't think or feel the way people do. It's a very fast pattern-matcher.

Some AI apps let you type or speak a question in plain words, and they answer like a person would. These are called AI chat assistants or chatbots. Well-known ones include ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI, and Grok.

docs.heading: What a patient portal is
docs.text:
A patient portal is a private website or app from your doctor's office or hospital. It's usually free. MyChart is one common example, but there are many others. Ask your doctor's office which one they use.
In a portal, you may be able to:
- See test results and visit notes
- Send a message to your care team (for things that aren't urgent)
- Make or check appointments
- Ask for a refill, or pay a bill

docs.text:

   - What you'll tap: The App Store (iPhone) or Google Play (Android). Search for the name they gave you. Check that the app is made by the right company.
2. Sign up. Tap Sign up or Create account. The office may give you an activation code. You'll also need your name and birthday.
3. Make a strong password. Your phone can save it for you. You may also get a code by text to prove it's you. Type that code only into the portal.
4. Find your results. Look for Test Results or Health. Tap a result to open it.
5. Send a message. Look for Messages, then New message or Ask a question. Type your question and tap Send.
6. Sign out when you're done, if you use a shared computer or tablet.

docs.heading: What a tampered card can look like
docs.text:
- The PIN is showing. The strip that covers the PIN on the back is scratched, peeled, wrinkled, or missing.
- The package is torn or opened. Look for rips, wrinkles, bends, or a pack that looks opened and sealed again.

- The card number is easy to see. If you can read the number and PIN in the store, so could someone else.

docs.heading: Before you buy: what to do
docs.text:
1. Pick a card from the back of the rack. Don't take the first card in front. The FBI says to try one from the middle or the back.
2. Look at both sides. Check the PIN strip, the pack, and the barcode.
   - What you'll do: Run your finger over the barcode on the back. A sticker on top can feel raised.
3. See a problem? Take a different card. Show the bad card to a cashier or manager. Thieves sometimes mess with a whole batch of cards, so you may want to shop at a different store.
4. Watch the screen at checkout. Ask the cashier to scan the card in front of you. Make sure the amount on the screen is right.
5. Keep your receipt. Take a picture of the card and the receipt with your phone. You'll need them if something goes wrong.
6. Pay with a credit card if you can. The FTC says a credit card gives you the most protection if there's a problem.
Other safe ways to buy: Some stores keep gift cards behind the counter or in a locked case. You can also buy a gift card online, right from the brand's own website. Type the address yourself. Don't buy gift cards from online auction sites. They may be fake or stolen.

docs.heading: Step 1: Take the Hearing Test (about 5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Charge your AirPods. Sit in a quiet room. Turn off fans and the TV.
2. Put your AirPods in your ears. Make sure they're connected to your iPhone.
3. Open Settings. Tap the name of your AirPods near the top.
   - What you'll tap: A gray gear icon, then a line like "Pat's AirPods Pro."
4. Tap Hearing Health, then Take a Hearing Test.
5. Follow the steps on screen. It may ask you to check the fit or try a different size of ear tip.
6. Tap the screen each time you hear a tone. Each tone plays three times. You only need to tap once. It's OK to miss some.
7. At the end, you'll see a number for each ear and what it means. Tap Show Details to see more. Your results are saved in the Health app.
Already have a hearing test from a professional? You can use those results instead. You'll see how in Step 2.

docs.heading: Hearing Protection for loud places
docs.text:
Hearing Protection lowers loud sounds around you, like at a concert, a ball game, or with a lawn mower. It's on by default whenever your AirPods are in a listening mode. Here's how to get the most from it:
1. Check the fit. Open Settings, tap the name of your AirPods, then Ear Tip Fit Test. A good seal blocks more noise.
2. Pick a listening mode. Press and hold the stem of an AirPod to switch modes:
   - Transparency: You still hear people around you, like at a concert.
   - Adaptive: For noise that comes and goes, like traffic.
   - Noise Cancellation: Blocks the most sound all the time.
3. Keep them charged. Hearing Protection doesn't work when the battery runs out. You'll hear a tone at 10 percent battery, and again just before they turn off.
Don't turn off Loud Sound Reduction. It's under Settings, then Accessibility, then AirPods. If it's off, Hearing Protection is off too.

docs.summary: Someone told you to pay with gift cards? It’s a scam. What to do, and how to try to get your money back.

docs.heading: How the scam usually goes
docs.text:
Gift card scams start with a call, text, email, or social media message. The person may say they're from the government, your bank, a company you know, or tech support. They may say you won a prize. They may say a family member is in trouble. Or they may be someone you met online who says they care about you.
Then the pattern is almost always the same:
1. They say it's urgent. Pay right now, or something terrible will happen. They don't want you to stop and think, or talk to someone you trust.
2. They tell you which cards to buy, and where. They may name Apple, Google Play, Amazon, Target, or eBay cards. They may send you to a certain store, or to several stores so the cashier won't get suspicious.
3. They stay on the phone with you. Some will stay on the line while you drive to the store and buy the cards. They act like they're helping you.
4. They ask for the numbers on the back. Once they have the card number and PIN, they can take the money, even though you still have the card.

docs.heading: What to do right now
docs.text:
1. Stop and hang up. Or close the message. You don't have to explain. It's okay to be "rude" to a stranger.
2. Don't buy the cards. If you already bought them, don't share the numbers and don't send a photo of the card.
3. Check with someone you trust. Call a family member or friend. If the person said they're from a company or agency, call it yourself. Use a number from your bill, the back of your card, or the official website. Don't use a number they gave you.

Good to know: Apple says its gift cards can only be used to buy things from Apple. They can't pay a bill, taxes, or a government fee. The same idea goes for other store gift cards.

Act fast. The money may still be on the card.

docs.heading: Signs it might be a scam
docs.text:
The FTC says to watch for these:
1. They rush you. "Give right now, today only." Real charities will still take your gift tomorrow.
2. They want cash, a gift card, a wire transfer, or crypto. That's how scammers ask to be paid. Don't do it.
3. They thank you for a gift you never made. It's a trick to get you to "finish" paying.
4. The name sounds almost like a charity you know. Scammers copy real names on purpose.
5. They're vague. Lots of sad stories, but no clear answer about how your money will be used.
6. They promise a prize. Winning a sweepstakes in exchange for a donation is a scam, and it's illegal.

docs.heading: How to check a charity in a few minutes
docs.text:
1. Ask questions first. What's the charity's exact name? Where is it? How will my money be used? A real charity will answer. You can also say, "Please send me something in writing."
2. Search the name online. Type the charity's name plus the word "scam," "complaint," or "review." See what other people say.
3. Look up its ratings. These free sites report on how charities spend money:
   - BBB Wise Giving Alliance
   - Charity Navigator
   - CharityWatch
4. Check that it's a real tax-exempt charity. Use the IRS's free Tax Exempt Organization Search. It also tells you if your gift can be tax-deductible.
5. Check with your state. Most states require charities to register before asking for money. Find your state's charity office at nasconet.org.
6. Go to the charity yourself. Want to give? Hang up, close the message, and go to the charity's real website or call a number you looked up. Don't use a link or number they sent you.

docs.heading: How the scam usually goes
docs.text:
The FTC, FBI, and AARP say these calls often follow the same story:
1. "Grandma, it's me." The caller cries or speaks softly, or says they have a broken nose or a bad line, to explain why they sound different. Some scammers use AI to copy a real voice.
2. Something terrible happened. They were arrested, were in a car crash, or got hurt on a trip. Scammers may name a place your family member really went, after seeing it on social media.
3. Someone "official" gets on the line. A "lawyer," "police officer," or "bail bondsman" tells you how much to pay.
4. "Please don't tell Mom and Dad." They may say there's a "gag order." Secrecy keeps you from checking.
5. They want money right now, and in a way that's hard to get back: cash, gift cards, a wire transfer, a payment app, or crypto.
Watch out for these two tricks:
- "Someone will come pick up the cash." The FBI warns that scammers send a courier, or even a ride-share driver, to your home to collect it.
- "Put the cash in the mail." The FTC says scammers tell people to hide bills between the pages of a magazine and mail them.
Good to know: Caller ID can be faked to show a name or number you trust. And AARP says real police don't call family members to collect bail money.

docs.heading: Set up a family safe word
docs.text:
A safe word (also called a code word) is a simple way to know it's really them. AARP and the FBI both suggest it.
1. Pick a word or short phrase that's easy to remember but hard to guess, like "blue pancakes." Don't use a pet's name or anything posted online.
2. Share it in person or by phone, not in a group text or on social media.
3. Agree on the rule: anyone who calls asking for money in an emergency must say the safe word.
4. No safe word? Hang up and call them back yourself.
Worried you'll forget the word? AARP suggests using a family story only your family would know instead.
A good time to set it up: when family visits for the holidays. It takes two minutes at the kitchen table.

docs.text:
When you talk to Gemini, Google can save your chats in your Google account. This is called Gemini Apps Activity. The setting that saves it is called Keep Activity.
- If you're 18 or over, Keep Activity is on unless you turn it off.
- By default, Google deletes your Gemini activity after 18 months. You can change this to 3 or 36 months.
To see or delete your Gemini activity:
1. On a computer, or in your phone's web browser, go to myactivity.google.com/product/gemini and sign in.
2. To delete, tap Delete, then choose Last hour, Last day, or All time.
3. To stop saving, tap On near the top, then Turn off (or Turn off and delete activity).
Before you turn it off, know this:
- Google says reminders and Google Tasks need Keep Activity on. With it off, voice reminders may stop working.
- Calls and texts by voice still work with it off.
- Even with it off, Google keeps your chats for up to 72 hours to run the service. They don't show in your activity.
Your choice: It's fine to leave it on or turn it off. Pick what feels right for you.
Old Google Assistant history isn't deleted on its own. You can find and delete it at myactivity.google.com.
Don't share private info, like passwords, bank numbers, or your Social Security number, with any AI helper.

docs.heading: Step 1: Turn on the battery saver
docs.text:
Every phone has a mode that makes the battery last longer. Your phone still makes calls, sends texts, and gets email. Some things just slow down or check for news less often.
iPhone (Low Power Mode):
1. Open Settings and tap Battery.
2. On iPhone 15 or newer, tap Power Mode, then Low Power Mode. On iPhone 14 or older, tap Low Power Mode right on the Battery screen.
   - What you'll see: The battery icon at the top turns yellow.
3. It turns off by itself once your phone charges to 80%.
Also on iPhone 15 Pro or newer: Adaptive Power is usually on already. It gently saves power on busy days and can turn on Low Power Mode for you at 20%. You'll find it in Settings, Battery, Power Mode.
Google Pixel and many other Android phones (Battery Saver):
1. Swipe down from the top of the screen.
2. Tap Battery Saver. (You may need to swipe down twice.)
3. To have it turn on by itself, open Settings, tap Battery, then Battery Saver, then Schedule and reminders. Turn on "Turn on based on battery level" and pick a level, such as 20%.
Good to know: While Battery Saver is on, a Pixel phone may stop listening for "Hey Google." Tap the button on screen instead.
Need a phone to last a day or more on a Pixel? Try Extreme Battery Saver (in Settings, Battery, Battery Saver). It pauses most apps, and paused apps don't send alerts. Phone, Messages, and Clock keep working. You can pick other apps to keep on under Essential apps.
Samsung Galaxy (Power saving):
1. Open Settings and tap Battery. (On older Galaxy phones, tap Battery and device care, then Battery.)
2. Turn on Power saving.
3. Tap the words Power saving to see what it changes, like a dimmer screen and a shorter screen timeout.

docs.text:
The bright screen is one of the biggest users of battery.
- Turn the brightness down a little. Swipe down from the top of the screen and slide the sun bar to the left. Keep it bright enough to read comfortably.

docs.heading: Step 3: Find out what's using your battery
docs.text:
Your phone keeps a list of which apps used the most battery. If one app you hardly use is near the top, that's your clue.
iPhone:
1. Open Settings and tap Battery.
2. Scroll down to see each app and the share of battery it used. Tap View All Battery Usage to see earlier days.
3. Tap an app for details. "Background" means it was working while you weren't looking at it, like playing music or getting mail.
Android (Pixel):
1. Open Settings, tap Battery, then Battery usage.
2. Tap View by apps.
3. Tap an app, then Allow background usage. Google suggests keeping "Optimized" on for every app.
What to do with a battery-hungry app:
- Turn off its alerts if you don't need them. Each alert wakes your phone up. Open Settings, find the app (on Android, tap Apps first), then tap Notifications and turn off the ones you don't want.
- Close it, or remove it if you never use it. On iPhone, Apple says a weak cell signal also uses more battery, so the list may show "Cellular coverage" when you were somewhere with poor service.

docs.heading: Step 4: Charge in a way that's kind to the battery
docs.text:
You don't need a special routine. A few simple habits help the battery last for years.
- Charging overnight is fine. Apple says your iPhone stops charging when it's full, so it's safe to leave it plugged in overnight.
- Leave the smart charging on. iPhone has Optimized Battery Charging, which is on unless you turned it off. Pixel phones have Adaptive Charging. Both wait to fill up the last bit until shortly before you usually unplug.
- Keep it cool. Apple says the best room temperature for an iPhone is 62° to 72° F (16° to 22° C). Heat above 95° F (35° C) can permanently shorten battery life. Google says the same thing: heat drains and damages the battery.
- Don't leave your phone in a parked car on a warm day, or in direct sun for a long time.
- Cold is different. In the cold, the battery may run down faster for a while. It goes back to normal once the phone warms up.
- Take off a thick case if your phone gets hot while it charges.
- Use a good charger. Google suggests the charger that came with your phone. Any charger should be from the phone maker or a well-known brand.
If your iPhone says "Charging On Hold": It's too hot or too cold to charge safely. Move it somewhere with a normal room temperature. It starts charging again by itself.

docs.heading: Step 4: Look at the plan list
docs.text:
You'll see a list of plans in your area. For each plan, the list shows things like:
- The monthly premium (what you pay each month to have the plan).
- The yearly drug and premium cost for the drugs you entered. This is an estimate.
- The deductible and the most you'd pay out of pocket.
- Star ratings from 1 to 5, for quality and service.
To learn more about one plan, tap Plan Details. You can see what each of your drugs costs and any rules for getting them.

docs.heading: Step 5: Compare plans side by side
docs.text:
1. Check Add to compare on up to 3 plans.
2. Tap the Compare button to see them next to each other.
3. Want a paper copy? Use the print button on the page, or your browser's print option.
Before you decide, call to check. It's a good idea to call the plan and make sure your doctors and pharmacy are in its network. Networks can change.

docs.heading: Step 6: Join a plan (only if you want to)
docs.text:
1. Tap Enroll on the plan you chose and follow the steps.
2. When you finish, you'll get a confirmation number. Write it down or print the page. Keep it in case something goes wrong.
3. The plan must get your request by December 7.
You can also join by calling the plan or 1-800-MEDICARE.

docs.heading: Stay safe from Medicare scams
docs.text:
- Medicare won't call you out of the blue to sell you a plan or ask for your Medicare number.
- Real Medicare websites end in .gov. Type Medicare.gov yourself.
- Don't give your Medicare number to a caller, a text, or a website you reached from an ad.
- Using Plan Finder and SHIP is free.
- Got a call you're not sure about? Hang up. Then call 1-800-MEDICARE yourself.
More warning signs are in our guide to Medicare scams.

docs.heading: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
- It logged me out while I was typing drugs. This can happen if you look without an account and wait too long. Start again and add your drugs a little faster, or sign in so your list saves.
- I can't find my drug. Try the generic name on your pill bottle. Some names are spelled out in full, like "hydrochloride" instead of "HCl."
- The drug costs look wrong. Check the dose, form, and how often you fill it. A small mistake there can change the cost a lot.
- This is too much. That's okay. A SHIP counselor can go through it with you for free, over the phone or in person. Find yours at shiphelp.org.
